relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.
tool_note.hashpipe: verified by round-tripping each type PINNED with -m, not by taking an unpinned report: hashpipe names the FIRST type that reproduces a digest, so an unpinned answer names a type that works and not necessarily this one.
tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.

entries.name: AxCrypt 2 AES-128
entries.notes: john has an AxCrypt 2.x format and it is NOT recorded here, because the measurement is ambiguous and a guess would be a false claim either way. Measured 2026-09-01: john --format=axcrypt2-opencl LOADS this entry's vector ("Loaded 1 password hash ... AxCrypt 2.x [PBKDF2-SHA512 AES OpenCL]") and then does not recover "hashcat" from it, while the same format recovers axcrypt-2-aes-256's vector on the first candidate. That is not a parse failure -- john accepted the hash and rejected the password -- so either john's format does not implement the AES-128 key wrap, or this vector is not what it says. The vector itself is sound: hashcat mode 23500 round-trips it, tier vector. Left open for upstream rather than resolved by picking a side.

The vector stored for mdxfind is mdxfind's own example rather than the transcode, because an independent credential is better evidence than the same one written twice.

The RAW type was dropped from this mapping on 2026-09-05 because it was never true. mdxfind revision 1.290 (2026-04-09) regressed the RAW family so that every RAW type became numerically identical to its plain sibling at x01 -- upstream's own words in revision 1.549, which restored the correct semantics on 2026-08-30. This row's vector is the PLAIN digest (or a truncation of one), so under the regression it verified as the RAW type as well, and the mapping reached tier `vector` on a coincidence rather than on the algorithm. The plain type remains and still verifies against the installed binary; nothing else on this row changes.

The same NAME means opposite things in john and mdxfind, which is what put this mapping on the wrong row. john's HMAC-* formats key on the PASSWORD -- john's own source says so, ALGORITHM_NAME is literally "password is key" in hmacMD5_fmt_plug.c, hmacSHA1_fmt_plug.c, hmacSHA256_fmt_plug.c and hmacSHA512_fmt_plug.c. mdxfind splits the two cases across two names: hx Appendix A gives HMAC-SHA1 (e215) as hmac_sha1(pass, user), keyed on the USER, and HMAC-SHA1-KPASS (e793) as hmac_sha1(salt, pass), keyed on the PASSWORD. So john's HMAC-SHA1 is mdxfind's HMAC-SHA1-KPASS, and matching the two by name pairs each with the wrong one.

relations.note: Measured 2026-09-04: this row and hmac-sha1-kpass are one computation under three names. john publishes the format HMAC-SHA1, hashcat publishes mode 150 "HMAC-SHA1 (key = $pass)" and mdxfind publishes the type HMAC-SHA1-KPASS, and mdxfind pinned to HMAC-SHA1-KPASS reproduces BOTH rows vectors -- this rows RFC 2202 vector once it is written in mdxfinds serialization (<digest>:<message>, plaintext = the key), and the other rows own vector, which already stands at tier vector. Note what the plain name does NOT mean: mdxfinds HMAC-SHA1 without the -KPASS suffix keys on the SALT and is already mapped to hmac-sha1-plain-salt (hashcat 160). The name match absence.pl reported for this row pointed at that type and was wrong.

tool_note.hashpipe: verified by round-tripping each type PINNED with -m, not by taking an unpinned report: hashpipe names the FIRST type that reproduces a digest, so an unpinned answer names a type that works and not necessarily this one.
tool_note.john: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-05: this row said john had no format for this computation, and john has had one all along. The same NAME means opposite things in john and mdxfind, which is what put this mapping on the wrong row. john's HMAC-* formats key on the PASSWORD -- john's own source says so, ALGORITHM_NAME is literally "password is key" in hmacMD5_fmt_plug.c, hmacSHA1_fmt_plug.c, hmacSHA256_fmt_plug.c and hmacSHA512_fmt_plug.c. mdxfind splits the two cases across two names: hx Appendix A gives HMAC-SHA1 (e215) as hmac_sha1(pass, user), keyed on the USER, and HMAC-SHA1-KPASS (e793) as hmac_sha1(salt, pass), keyed on the PASSWORD. So john's HMAC-SHA1 is mdxfind's HMAC-SHA1-KPASS, and matching the two by name pairs each with the wrong one. john's HMAC-SHA1 recovers this row's own plaintext from its own vector once that vector is written in john's <message>#<digest> shape. Superseded note follows. || no format. Swept the 33 format(s) whose own valid() accepts this entry's own vector, as john --show=left reports them, on 2026-09-04 (a tools/discover-john.pl sweep, evidence read by tools/absence.pl): not one reproduced this entry's own vector. That the vector was IN the search is not assumed -- the same sweep reported a hit on another vector of the same shape, a positive control measured in the same run by the same binary, and without it finding nothing would not be evidence. For john the control is also per ENTRY and not only per shape: every format counted above is one whose own loader ACCEPTED this hash, so each was asked this exact question and answered no. A format that cannot parse the hash is not counted at all, and an entry no format can parse is reported as unsearched rather than decided. Every applicable format ran to completion; a format killed at the timeout is counted as untested and withholds this verdict. No john format name matches any identifier this entry publishes either, normalized by the separator-drift rule. This is the absence of an IDENTIFIER, not of the algorithm: if john gains one, this becomes a mapping.

entries.expr_note: john publishes this as "HMAC-SHA224" and no category, so what kind of construction it is has not been established here. Its name is not expression-shaped and john's dynamic EXPRESSION language cannot be handed it, so there is no expression on this row. That says nothing about whether any tool can CRACK it, and it is not a claim that the algorithm HAS no expression -- run seed-hx.pl and derive-expressions.pl, which can settle that from evidence.

They are not independent evidence -- do not read two agreeing vectors here as corroboration. hashcat writes $krb5asrep$<et>$<user>$<REALM>$<checksum>$<data>; john writes $krb5asrep$<et>$<REALM><user>$<data>$<checksum>. The re-encoding was not assumed: each transcoded string was handed to john with only the plaintext the hashcat vector already states, and fell under both the CPU format and the GPU build.

tool_note.hashcat: hashcat's own published example hash for this mode, recovered by hashcat at this mode with hashcat's own published plaintext.
tool_note.john: GPU build(s) krb5asrep-aes-opencl proven on 2026-09-01 by cracking this entry's own vector(s) under that exact format; john ships no CPU format of that name, so discover-john.pl --mirror-gpu could not place them. CPU format krb5asrep added the same day and on the same evidence: it loads and cracks the transcoded vector too. john covers etypes 17, 18 and 23 under this one identifier, which is why kerberos-5-as-rep-etype-17-18-23 names it as well.
tool_note.mdxfind: no type. Swept all 1002 mdxfind types on 2026-09-03 (a tools/discover-mdxfind.pl sweep, evidence read by tools/absence.pl): not one reproduced this entry's own vector. That the vector was IN the search is not assumed -- the same sweep reported a hit on another vector of the same shape, a positive control measured in the same run by the same binary, and without it finding nothing would not be evidence. Every applicable type ran to completion; a type killed at the timeout is counted as untested and withholds this verdict. No mdxfind type name matches any identifier this entry publishes either, normalized by the separator-drift rule. Corroborated by hashpipe, a second binary built from the same catalog: handed this entry's own hash and plaintext it names no type at all. It is the more direct instrument -- it recomputes rather than cracking -- and on this corpus it named a type for 58 entries the sweep alone called silent. This is the absence of an IDENTIFIER, not of the algorithm: if mdxfind gains one, this becomes a mapping.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD4UTF16SHA1HUM (e576) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. entries.denotation: MD5SQL5-32 is MULTI-EMIT: it emits EIGHT digests per candidate and matches any of them. They are md5() of the MySQL5 digest written as upper-case hex and as lower-case hex, each taken four ways -- "1*" plus its first 30 characters, "*" plus 31, "*" plus 32, and the bare 32. This row name and its seven aliases are exactly those eight forms.
entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02. This row carried md5(cut($c1.upper(sha1(sha1_raw($p))),0,32)),c1=* at tier upstream, transcribed from hx Appendix A for e342. It is one of EIGHT forms and so a false claim on its own: mdxfind type MD5SQL5-32 is MULTI-EMIT. mdxfind.c JOB_MD5SQL5_32 writes the MySQL5 digest of the candidate as upper-case hex into mdbuf and as lower-case hex into linebuf, each behind the two bytes "1*", then fills mdcur[0..7] with md5 of four placements in each case: "1*" plus 30 characters, "*" plus 31, "*" plus 32, and the bare 32; it checkhash()es all eight every iteration. mdxfind -z counts exactly 8 emissions, RCS 1.545, measured 2026-09-02. This row already carried all eight as its name plus seven aliases, which is what nobody had connected.
entries.name: md5("1*".substr(mysql5($plain),0,30))

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. entries.denotation: MD5BASE64MD5RAWMD5 is MULTI-EMIT: it matches either md5(base64(md5_raw(md5($p)))) or md5(cut(base64(md5_raw(md5($p))),0,22)), which is the same base64 with its "==" padding removed
entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02. This row carried md5(base64(md5_raw(md5($p)))) at tier upstream, transcribed from hx Appendix A for e243, and triage recorded it as reproducing 1 of 2 vectors. Both vectors are correct and the expression was the false claim: mdxfind type MD5BASE64MD5RAWMD5 is MULTI-EMIT, so no single expression describes it. mdxfind.c b64md5raw computes md5 of the whole 24-character base64 into mdcur[0] and, under if (len > 18), md5 of the same base64 minus its last two characters into mdcur[1], then checkhash()es both. mdxfind -z counts 2 emissions for this type, RCS 1.545, measured 2026-09-02. mdxfind own hx VM reproduces this row first vector from the padded form and its second from the 22-character form, so the two vectors corroborate the type rather than contradicting each other.

entries.denotation: MD5CAPMD5USER is MULTI-EMIT: it matches either md5(cap(md5($p)).$u) or md5(cap(md5($p)).":".$u)
entries.expr_note: john's dynamic expression language has no literal-string token: --format=dynamic='md5(md5($p).":".$s)' fails with 'Invalid token following the . character' (checked 2026-08-31), so this construction cannot be written as an expression. That is separate from whether john has a FORMAT for it.
entries.name: md5(cap(md5($plain)).":".$username)
entries.notes: This row is mdxfind type MD5CAPMD5USER. CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-31, and the second correction matters more than the first. Waffle named the unknown vector d4f7dec5...:abc123 as the colon form, confirmed here by independent Digest::MD5 and by local mdxfind pinned to ^MD5CAPMD5USER$ with -F. But the hx specification (rev 1.15) Appendix A Note [24] then showed the stronger fact: MD5CAPMD5USER is a MULTI-EMIT type. It emits BOTH md5(cap(md5($p)).$u) and md5(cap(md5($p)).":".$u) and matches if either reproduces the stored digest. So this row is not one computation, and neither of its two vectors is anomalous -- 05b56c69... is the colonless emit and d4f7dec5... is the colon emit. The first correction here wrongly called the colonless vector foreign and removed it; it is restored. A copy also sits on md5-md5-pass-salt, which is the row for the colonless construction in its own right. john has no format for either emit: discover-john.pl ran all 957 formats against the colon vector with zero matches, and the dynamic language has no literal-string token. The 198,534-construction sweep that failed to identify this missed it because it enumerated terms and never a literal separator.

relations.note: MD5MD5USER and MD5CAPMD5USER differ only by cap() on the inner hex digest, which is a no-op whenever that digest starts with a digit. md5('rosetta') is 975790df..., so both types reproduce this shared vector identically; they diverge on any plaintext whose md5 starts with a letter.

entries.notes: This row is mdxfind type MD5MD5USER. CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-31, and the second correction matters more than the first. Waffle named the unknown vector d4f7dec5...:abc123 as the colon form, confirmed here by independent Digest::MD5 and by local mdxfind pinned to ^MD5MD5USER$ with -F. The vector is right and was never in doubt; the DEPTH LABEL was wrong, inherited from a binary that reported the base one round early. mdxfind revision 1.290 (2026-04-09) regressed the RAW family -- "the base was reported one round early, so x01 became X(pass) instead of X(X_bin(pass))" -- and revision 1.549 (2026-08-30) restored it. Measured 2026-09-05: this entry's own stored vector reproduces under mdxfind RCS 1.576 at x01, and `hashpipe -c` pinned to the same type independently reports x01. It reproduced at x02 only under the regressed RCS 1.545, which is where the 2 came from. Note what this ALSO settles: hashpipe's john_map.h has published x01 for these types all along, and data/upstream-disagreements.yaml recorded that as an "iteration-numbering" convention difference. It was not a convention difference; it was this bug, and upstream's map was right.

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type MD51SALTMD5MD5 (e285) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.
entries.name: md5(md5(md5($plain)).$salt)

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type MD5-MD5MD5PASSSALT-PEP (e819) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

tool_note.mdxfind: `iterations` was corrected from 2 to 1 on 2026-09-05. The vector is right and was never in doubt; the DEPTH LABEL was wrong, inherited from a binary that reported the base one round early. mdxfind revision 1.290 (2026-04-09) regressed the RAW family -- "the base was reported one round early, so x01 became X(pass) instead of X(X_bin(pass))" -- and revision 1.549 (2026-08-30) restored it. Measured 2026-09-05: this entry's own stored vector reproduces under mdxfind RCS 1.576 at x01, and `hashpipe -c` pinned to the same type independently reports x01. It reproduced at x02 only under the regressed RCS 1.545, which is where the 2 came from. Note what this ALSO settles: hashpipe's john_map.h has published x01 for these types all along, and data/upstream-disagreements.yaml recorded that as an "iteration-numbering" convention difference. It was not a convention difference; it was this bug, and upstream's map was right.

entries.expr_note: Withdrawn 2026-08-31. This entry carried the expression "md5(md5(md5($p).$s).pepper)", transcribed from the hx Language Specification $Revision: 1.15$ (Waffle, Aug 2026), Appendix A entry for mdxfind type MD5-MD5MD5PASSSALT-PEP (e819) by a parser that has since been corrected: it carries the bare operand pepper, which john's dynamic language cannot bind. Nothing can compile that string, so it was a claim rather than a fact, and it is withdrawn rather than adjusted -- guessing what upstream meant is exactly what the expression field exists to stop. Re-run seed-hx.pl and denote-hx.pl to settle this entry from the corrected parse. Settled here: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type MD5-MD5MD5PASSSALT-PEP (e819) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: Withdrawn 2026-08-31. This entry carried the expression "md5($s.sha1(pepper.$p))", transcribed from the hx Language Specification $Revision: 1.15$ (Waffle, Aug 2026), Appendix A entry for mdxfind type MD5-SALT-SHA1PEPPASS (e822) by a parser that has since been corrected: it carries the bare operand pepper, which john's dynamic language cannot bind. Nothing can compile that string, so it was a claim rather than a fact, and it is withdrawn rather than adjusted -- guessing what upstream meant is exactly what the expression field exists to stop. Re-run seed-hx.pl and denote-hx.pl to settle this entry from the corrected parse. Settled here: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type MD5-SALT-SHA1PEPPASS (e822) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02: this entry read cap(md5($p)), transcribed from the hx specification's Appendix A for mdxfind type MD5CAP (e353). That string is wrong twice over, and Appendix A is wrong about this type in the same way CLAUDE.md already records for e308. mdxfind.c JOB_MD5CAP capitalizes mdbuf[0] ONLY (if (islower(mdbuf[0]))), where hx's bare cap() moves the first lower-case LETTER anywhere; and its loop is for (x = 2; x <= Maxiter; x++) with checkhash INSIDE, so the type never emits a one-iteration value -- mdxfind -i 1 pinned to this type matches nothing. The replacement was established three independent ways, all agreeing on this entry's own vector: the source, the binary reporting it as MD5CAPx02 at -i 2, and hx evaluating md5(cap(md5(pass), 0)). Stays tier upstream because john's dynamic language has no cap() token, so no round-trip can ever promote it. The other twelve cap() entries are NOT affected: five of them carry vectors that discriminate between the two readings and all five match hx's bare cap(), so e353 is an outlier rather than a family error.; TRIAGE 2026-09-04 [corroborated]: no john format, so john ships no control vectors; but RosettaExpr -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes this expression over the entry's own vector(s) and reproduces 1 of 1. That is corroboration, not tier vector, which needs john's own compiler
entries.name: MD5CAP

relations.note: MD5CAP is md5(cap(md5($p),0)) and its cap() touches position 0 only, so whenever the inner digest does not START with a lower-case letter the type is byte-identical to two-iteration plain MD5 -- which is how john's dynamic_2 and plain MD5 crack its vector without denoting it. Corrected 2026-09-02 from a note that described hx's bare cap() (first lower-case letter anywhere), a different function that this type does not use.

entries.name: MD5SPECAM
entries.notes: mdxfind and hashpipe do NOT compute the same thing under this name, measured 2026-09-04, and the vector on this row is hashpipe's. hashpipe's compute_md5specam is md5($p . md5_raw($p)) -- it takes neither salt nor user (it is registered with flags 0 and casts both away) -- and its published example 9018942a51656d6055f0c20024dd4f48:password123 was confirmed three independent ways: hashpipe -c pinned to MD5SPECAM, the source itself, and a recomputation in Perl. mdxfind's JOB_MD5SPECAM (mdxfind.c, the case at ~27795) reads a USERID off the line, lower-casing it up to the first colon, and breaks out when that field is empty -- it is a member of the AM family, whose sibling MD5AM hashpipe's own source records as md5(user . "::" . lower($p)). Pinned with -h '^MD5SPECAM$', mdxfind performs ZERO hash calculations on this line under -f and zero again under -F with a userid field appended, so it is declining the input shape rather than computing and missing. The mdxfind mapping therefore stays at tier `asserted`: what is on this row is proven for hashpipe's MD5SPECAM and says nothing yet about mdxfind's.

tool_note.mdxfind: special purpose and not for general use, per mdxfind's maintainer, and it emits nothing. Measured 2026-09-04, pinned with -M under -z: alone, with -s and with -u, stdout was empty in every case, and a run seeded from mdxfind's own regress/md5specamdef.txt produced nothing either. So MDXFIND can generate no vector for it and the mdxfind mapping cannot reach tier vector; that is a property of mdxfind's type rather than a gap here. Narrowed from "this entry cannot reach tier vector" on 2026-09-04: hashpipe ships an example for a type of the same name and it verifies, so the row now carries a vector. See notes: -- the two tools do not compute the same thing under this name, which does not touch the measurement above. The identifier is real and in mdxfind's type table, which is what the mapping records.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD5UCBASE64MD5RAW (e375) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.
entries.name: MD5UCBASE64MD5RAW

tool_note.hashpipe: hashpipe e375 MD5UCBASE64MD5RAW. verified with hashpipe -c, which pins each line to its own leading TYPE label and runs no detection, at -t 1 and with the emitted label compared against the one asked for. Both precautions matter on this build: -m does not restrict what a recognised wrapper reaches, and results vary with the thread count. No iterations: is recorded from hashpipe -- the suffixes are different quantities and this repository follows mdxfind for that field.

entries.notes: The vendored catalog renders this type's example digest in uppercase hex, and mdxfind will not read it back in that case, so the seeding pass could not verify it. mdxfind -z computes the same digest in lowercase for the same plaintext, and pinned to ^MD5UCBASE64SHA1RAW$ it reproduces that form; the stored vector is the catalog's own digest re-cased, not one we invented. Fourteen other types carry an uppercase example (MD5UC, SHA1UC, SHA256UC, RACF, ORACLE7 among them) and are NOT all the same story -- MD5UC and SHA256UC do not reproduce in either case.

entries.name: MS Office 2016 - SheetProtection
entries.notes:
WHERE THE HASH LIVES. This is not document encryption and office2john does
not extract it. An .xlsx is a zip; the digest is a cleartext attribute run
on the protection element of the relevant part:

    <sheetProtection algorithmName="SHA-512" hashValue="..."
                     saltValue="..." spinCount="100000" sheet="1"/>

THE ATTRIBUTE NAMES ARE NOT UNIFORM, which is where a naive extractor goes
wrong. `<sheetProtection>`, `<chartsheetProtection>` and `<fileSharing>` use
the bare names above. `<workbookProtection>` carries TWO INDEPENDENT digests
under PREFIXED names: workbookAlgorithmName / workbookHashValue /
workbookSaltValue / workbookSpinCount for the structure password, and
revisionsAlgorithmName / revisionsHashValue / revisionsSaltValue /
revisionsSpinCount for the revisions password. Word's
`<w:documentProtection>`, `<w:writeProtection>` and `<w:modifyVerifier>` use
the bare names again, namespace-prefixed.

Measured 2026-09-03: sheetProtection, fileSharing and BOTH prefixed
workbookProtection slots round-trip at mode 25300, against fixtures whose
attribute spellings come from openpyxl's own schema classes rather than from
recollection. The Word elements were exercised only against a hand-written
.docx, so those spellings remain spec reading and not measurement.

THE HASHCAT LINE is built from three of those attributes and two literals:

    $office$2016$0$<spinCount>$<saltValue>$<hashValue>

`2016` and `0` never vary; salt precedes hash; both go in base64 exactly as
the XML spells them. Getting the order wrong or using ':' as the separator
produces hashcat's "separator unmatched", which reads like a corrupt hash
rather than a malformed line.

HASHCAT'S PARSER IS STRICTER THAN THE FILE FORMAT, and its error names the
wrong field. src/modules/module_25300.c in v7.1.2-549 requires the spinCount
token to be six digits AND to equal 100000 (line 165), the salt to be
exactly 24 base64 characters decoding to 16 bytes, and the digest exactly 88
decoding to 64. Probed against the binary across ten spin values on
2026-09-03: only 100000 loads, and every other value is rejected as
"Salt-value exception", which sends the reader off to inspect the salt.
Excel's own default is 100000 so most real files pass, but a document
written with any other spin count has a real, well-formed SHA-512 digest and
NO hashcat mode at all.

THE CONSTRUCTION, measured 2026-09-03 by reproducing hashcat's own example
vector above with all four plausible orderings and finding exactly one
match:

    H_0 = SHA512(saltValue . utf16le(password))
    H_i = SHA512(H_{i-1} . uint32le(i-1))   for i = 1 .. spinCount
    hashValue = base64(H_spinCount)

The counter is APPENDED and 0-BASED. Agile ENCRYPTION prepends it, and that
difference is the whole trap: the prepending order computes a perfectly
well-formed digest that simply is not this one, with nothing to indicate the
error. It is SHA-512 throughout, not SHA-256; secondary write-ups say SHA-256
and are wrong. hashcat's 25300 kernel is SHA-512 only, so a file whose
algorithmName is anything else has no mode.

Proven end to end on 2026-09-03 against a synthesized .xlsx carrying a
SHA-512 sheetProtection element for a known password, extracted from the
XML and cracked by hashcat at this mode.

The pre-2013 form of the same feature is a 16-bit verifier in a `password`
attribute, which is a different algorithm and has its own entry:
ms-office-sheetprotection-legacy. And for either form, note that the file is
not encrypted -- deleting the protection element and rezipping opens the
sheet, so cracking is only warranted when the password itself is the object.

entries.alias: Excel sheet protection password; Excel workbook protection password; sheetProtection password attribute; BIFF Password/Protect record; Binary Document Password Verifier Derivation Method 1
entries.application: Microsoft Excel <=2010 file format; still written by openpyxl and by LibreOffice
entries.denotation: Binary Document Password Verifier Derivation Method 1
entries.expr_note: the construction is a 15-bit rotate-and-xor over the password read BACKWARDS, then an xor of the length and of the constant 0xCE4B. john's dynamic expression vocabulary has no rotate, no xor and no reversal, so this cannot be written as an expression at all -- that is a lookup against the function names in john's own --list=subformats, not an opinion. It is also separate from whether john can CRACK it, and john cannot: see tools.john.
entries.name: MS Office SheetProtection - legacy 16-bit verifier
entries.notes:
A 16-bit password verifier, not a hash in any useful sense. In an OOXML part
it appears under a DIFFERENT ATTRIBUTE NAME on each element: `password` on
`<sheetProtection>` and `<chartsheetProtection>`, `workbookPassword` and
`revisionsPassword` on `<workbookProtection>` (two independent passwords on
one element), and `reservationPassword` on `<fileSharing>`. Spellings taken
from openpyxl's schema classes and exercised 2026-09-03. It is also the data
of the BIFF PASSWORD and PROTECT records in a pre-2007 .xls. The native form
-- the one the vector
above is written in -- is FOUR HEXADECIMAL DIGITS exactly as the attribute
spells them, with no wrapper, no salt and no iteration count, because there
is nowhere for any of those to go.

The algorithm, from MS-OFFCRYPTO 2.3.7.1: start at 0; for each character of
the password taken from LAST to FIRST, rotate the running value left within
15 bits and xor the character code; then rotate once more, xor the password
length, and xor the constant 0xCE4B. Reimplemented and measured 2026-09-03
against the value openpyxl 3.0.9 writes for "P@ssw0rd", which is the vector
above.

BYTE ORDER IS A TRAP. The XML attribute and the BIFF record render the same
word in opposite orders, so published write-ups give "AB94" for the value
this repository records as "94AB". They are the same verifier. Check which
container a quoted value came out of before comparing it to anything.

THE ORIGINAL PASSWORD IS NOT RECOVERABLE and no tool will ever make it so:
16 bits cannot carry it. What is recoverable is a COLLIDING password, which
unlocks the sheet just as well. Measured 2026-09-03: 'DbOUJLIb' verifies to
94AB, found in 24065 random 8-character tries in under a second. Do not
report such a string as the password.

Collisions are dense but NOT uniformly reachable, which is the practical
gotcha. Exhausting printable ASCII at lengths 1 to 4 -- 82,317,120 strings
-- reaches only 1536 distinct verifier values out of 65536, and 94AB is not
among them, because a short password is rotated too few times for the high
bits ever to be set. Search at the same length as the original or longer; a
short-candidate sweep can return nothing and prove nothing.

Operationally, cracking is usually the wrong move for either form of sheet
protection. The file is not encrypted: deleting the protection element and
rezipping opens the sheet, and only a genuine interest in the password
itself (credential reuse, an investigation) justifies the rest.

entries.notes: john reads BOTH tools' NTLMv2 serializations: measured 2026-09-01, netntlmv2 and ntlmv2-opencl load and crack this entry's hashcat-form vectors (USER::DOMAIN:challenge:response:blob) unchanged. An earlier run of this session reported "No password hashes loaded" and three re-serialized vectors were briefly added on that basis; the cause was a --field-separator-char=tab passed by the probing tool, which governs how john splits LOGIN from HASH when READING a file, so a tab made john treat each whole line as one login. The vectors were withdrawn and the tool fixed. Kerberos AS-REP is NOT like this: john genuinely cannot read hashcat's $krb5asrep$ field order, which is why those rows do carry a transcoded vector. Two reasons this block is still tier asserted, neither of which is doubt about NETNTLMv2 itself. (1) It names netlmv2, a DIFFERENT computation, and a block carries one tier for every identifier in it; netlmv2 recovers none of these vectors, and the fourth vector (aTest:::...:A1E7281FE8C10E53, an 8-byte blob far short of an NTLMv2 one) looks like the NETLMv2 one. That is a row holding two computations, which CLAUDE.md forbids, and splitting it is curation. (2) verify-vectors.pl cannot check this format at all: it writes a synthetic login and a TAB before each hash, which is right for a hash that is only a digest and wrong here, because a NETNTLMv2 ciphertext EMBEDS its own login (USER::DOMAIN:...) and john will not parse it once that field has been displaced. Measured 2026-09-01: the same vectors load and crack under netntlmv2 and ntlmv2-opencl when handed to john natively, 3 of 4, and verify-vectors.pl reports 0 of 4 for all three identifiers.

entries.expr_note: CORRECTED 2026-09-02. This row previously carried sha1(utf16be(upper($p))), transcribed from the hx specification Appendix A entry for mdxfind type PEOPLESOFT (e858). Appendix A is wrong TWICE there: the encoding is UTF-16LE, not BE, and there is no upper() at all. mdxfind SOURCE settles it and outranks the document -- mdxfind.c JOB_PEOPLESOFT (line 20644) converts the candidate through iconv descriptor cd, opened UTF-8 to UTF-16LE//IGNORE at line 11690, then mysha1() then b64_encode() of 20 bytes, with no case folding anywhere. Corroborated four further ways, all 2026-09-02: mdxfind own hx VM, built -DHX_STANDALONE from the same tree, evaluates base64(sha1_bin(utf16le(pass))) to this row own vector byte for byte INCLUDING the = padding; an independent Perl recomputation (Digest::SHA + MIME::Base64) reproduces it and reproduces NEITHER of Appendix A two errors; hashcat -m 133 already round-trips this vector; and john dynamic compiler cracks the same digest under dynamic=sha1_64(utf16($p)). The tier stays upstream and not vector because john _64 flavor emits UNPADDED base64, so john was handed lACuKESOE2QXTd4mmyzOG8qdfug with the trailing = stripped -- a transcode of the stored ciphertext, not this row own hash, and mdxfind loader requires that padding (len == 28 and line[27] == = at mdxfind.c line 43971). Anyone running the john_dynamic_expr on the stored vector must strip the = first or john will not load it.; TRIAGE 2026-09-04 [corroborated]: no john format, so john ships no control vectors; but RosettaExpr -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes this expression over the entry's own vector(s) and reproduces 1 of 1. That is corroboration, not tier vector, which needs john's own compiler

entries.notes: Created 2026-09-04. This corpus had no row for plain SHA-1 as such, which is what blocked resolving the two-computations problem on sha1-substr-0-32: john's Raw-SHA1 sits on aich, sha1uc and netscape-ldap, and the truncation row held mdxfind's SHA1, so deleting the plain-SHA-1 claims there would have stranded them rather than rehomed them. They are rehomed here.

relations.note: sha1-substr-0-32 is this computation cut to its first 32 hex characters. Split out of that row on 2026-09-04 by Royce's decision: it was carrying both, and only john's dynamic_1023 truncates. Every identifier here computes plain SHA-1 and no cut, and every one of them was round-tripped against this vector before the split -- nothing was re-tiered by moving it.

relations.note: Measured 2026-09-04: the same computation, sha1($salt.$pass), stored two ways. Django writes sha1$<salt>$<digest> and mdxfind reads <digest>:<salt>, and this rows own vector reproduces under mdxfind pinned to SHA1SALTPASS once it is rewritten that way, handed to mdxfind with only the plaintext this row already states. entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type SHA11SALTMD5 (e311) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type SHA1MD5MD5PASS (e663) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1-PEPPER-MD5SALT (e677) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: Withdrawn 2026-08-31. This entry carried the expression "sha1(utf16($s.rev(lower($p)).pepper))", transcribed from the hx Language Specification $Revision: 1.15$ (Waffle, Aug 2026), Appendix A entry for mdxfind type SHA1-SALT-UTF16-PEPPER (e446) by a parser that has since been corrected: it carries the bare operand pepper, which john's dynamic language cannot bind. Nothing can compile that string, so it was a claim rather than a fact, and it is withdrawn rather than adjusted -- guessing what upstream meant is exactly what the expression field exists to stop. Re-run seed-hx.pl and denote-hx.pl to settle this entry from the corrected parse. Settled here: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1-SALT-UTF16-PEPPER (e446) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: CORRECTED 2026-09-02. This row previously carried sha1($p), on the reading that dynamic_1023 truncates the STORAGE and the expression describes the computation. Withdrawn for one reason: the expression is this repository join key, and axcryptsha1 (mdxfind e916) already spells the identical construction as cut(sha1($p),0,32). Two rows for one computation that spell it differently do not join, which is the entire point of the field. The cut is also what this row own name, its legacy hashes_org name CUT0-32SHA1, and john own --list=subformats all say: john states dynamic_1023 as "sha1($p) (hash truncated to length 32)", for an identifier this row proved by round-trip. mdxfind hx VM, built -DHX_STANDALONE 2026-09-02, evaluates cut(sha1(pass),0,32) to d21af7ece046af0e12d3c38472792cd5, this row first vector, exactly. Tier stays upstream and cannot become vector: cut() has no john dynamic spelling at all (RosettaJohn %NO_JOHN), so john compiler can never be handed this string, and john_dynamic_expr has been WITHDRAWN for the same reason -- the dynamic=sha1($p) it used to carry runs happily and produces the 40-hex digest, not the 32-hex ciphertext stored here. CAVEAT, unresolved and left for a curator: this row second vector is the FULL 40-hex sha1("rosetta") and does not satisfy this expression, and hashcat -m 100, mdxfind SHA1, john dynamic_26 and raw-SHA1-opencl are all plain-SHA1 identifiers that compute no cut. See the curation note in notes:.; TRIAGE 2026-09-04 [compiler-cannot]: the expression is correct -- computed here with Digest:: it reproduces all 6 of john's own test vectors for dynamic_1023 -- and john's ad-hoc compiler still recovers none of them, so the string is right and --format=dynamic cannot execute it
entries.name: SHA1.Substr(0, 32)
entries.notes: RESOLVED 2026-09-04 by Royce, and the reasoning is kept because the shape recurs. This row was being asked to be two computations: its expression is cut(sha1($p),0,32), its 32-hex vector satisfies it, and the 40-hex sha1("rosetta") it also carried did not. Only john's dynamic_1023 truncates; the other five identifiers computed plain SHA-1. Nothing recorded here was ever false -- they had all been round-tripped -- they simply belonged to a different computation, and there was no row for it. There is now: see the sha1 entry, which took them and the 40-hex vector. No id changed and no claim was dropped.

relations.note: Both compute cut(sha1(pass),0,32); mdxfind hx VM reproduces each row own vector from that one string, 2026-09-02. They stay separate rows because the ciphertext SERIALIZATION differs: AxCrypt stores it behind a $axcrypt_sha1$ prefix and hashcat gives that its own mode 13300, where this row stores the bare 32 hex characters. Same computation, two encodings, two identifiers a reader can arrive by.

This row is sha1 cut to its first 32 hex characters. RESOLVED 2026-09-04 by Royce: the plain-SHA-1 identifiers this row carried -- hashcat 100, mdxfind SHA1, hashpipe SHA1, john dynamic_26 and raw-SHA1-opencl -- compute no cut and moved to the new sha1 row with the 40-hex vector they were proven against. Note what is NOT a mapping: mdxfind's SHA1 and hashpipe's SHA1 do recover the 32-hex vector, because mdxfind compares at the length of the shortest hash it loaded and cracking a truncated digest is a capability it has by design. That is the tool being able to crack this, not the tool having an identifier for the truncation, and "mdxfind -h '^SHA1$'" is still the command for it.

tool_note.john: dynamic_1023 is the only identifier on this row that truncates; john states it as "sha1($p) (hash truncated to length 32)". The plain-SHA-1 identifiers this row used to carry moved to the sha1 entry on 2026-09-04.

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type SHA11SALTMD5SHA256 (e763) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.
entries.name: SHA11SALTMD5SHA256

relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. SHA1lsb35 masks exactly 5 nibbles, so either blind spot covers the whole difference: the digests are identical from position 5 onward.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1MD5SALTPASSPEPPER (e607) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.
entries.name: SHA1MD5SALTPASSPEPPER
entries.notes: The vector here is NOT the one mdxfind's published catalog carries. mdxfind 1.543 (2026-08-29) changed what e607 computes: the old code staged the inner digest at linebuf+saltlen while writing the pepper at a fixed offset 32, so for any non-empty salt the hash covered the salt, then a TRUNCATED digest, then the pepper, and the output depended on the salt length. dlr's own note says any hash cracked as e607 before that revision will not verify against it. The catalog example 786aab530907a783e9c25a2c7326ab7907ebf798 is the PRE-FIX digest and was still being published on 2026-09-02, so it is upstream's stale artefact rather than a vector this row should carry. Replaced 2026-09-02 with the repaired construction sha1(md5(salt . pass) . pepper), established three independent ways: the source at RCS 1.545, a Digest:: recomputation in perl that reproduces 786aab... under the old layout and 0992047f... under the new, and the rebuilt binary cracking 0992047f... The salt field holds SALT then PEPPER, space separated, both 1122334455667788 here; a pepper is a site-wide secret that appears in no hash, so mdxfind reads it from a file (-j).

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type SHA1MD5TRUNCSALT (e683) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.name: SHA1SALTCX
entries.notes: This row has NO vector and that is a deliberate withholding, measured 2026-09-04. The only example anyone publishes for this type -- mdxfind's own inventory row and the vendored hashpipe catalog carry the same string -- b59b77c52921e5df0d007fec2518e0f726ce3aaf:administrator:password123, is a TEN-ITERATION hash, and this row declares no iteration count, which the schema reads as one. Both oracles agree and each refuses the wrong depth: hashpipe -c asked for SHA1SALTCXx01 refuses and emits SHA1SALTCXx10 when asked bare, and mdxfind -h '^SHA1SALTCX$' -i 1 finds nothing while -i 10 reproduces the line exactly, as SHA1SALTCXx10. Storing it here would put an x10 digest under an x01 row, which is the defect audit-iterations.pl exists to catch -- the iteration suffix is identity, not a tuning knob. The type does support depth 1 (hashpipe's source notes it verifies at every depth, x01 included); nobody has published a depth-1 example, and one generated locally could not promote mdxfind anyway. So this needs a curator: either a depth-1 vector from upstream, or a decision that this row is about SHA1SALTCXx10 and should say so. Worth reporting upstream: the catalog publishes a depth-10 example with nothing in the row to say the depth is not 1.

entries.denotation: SHA1SHA11CAP is MULTI-EMIT: it emits sha1() of the inner sha1 hex digest with each lower-case hex character upper-cased in turn, plus one form per letter a-f with every occurrence of that letter upper-cased. The number of emissions varies with the digest; it was 22 for "rosetta".
entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02. This row carried sha1(cap(sha1($p))) at tier upstream, transcribed from hx Appendix A for e737. That is ONE of 22 forms and so a false claim on its own: mdxfind type SHA1SHA11CAP is MULTI-EMIT. mdxfind.c JOB_SHA1SHA11CAP upper-cases each lower-case hex character of the inner sha1 digest IN TURN, emitting sha1 of each result, then upper-cases ALL occurrences of each letter a-f and emits six more. For the plaintext "rosetta" that is 16 + 6, and a full sweep of all 1002 types with mdxfind -z measured exactly 22 on 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The count is INPUT-DEPENDENT -- it follows how many lower-case hex letters the inner digest happens to have -- which settles it on its own: no single expression can describe a type whose number of candidates varies with the candidate. hx cap() means the FIRST lower-case letter only, which is just the first of the 22.

relations.note: SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. SHA1lsb35 masks exactly 5 nibbles, so either blind spot covers the whole difference: the digests are identical from position 5 onward.

tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.

tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.

entries.notes: The vector is hashpipe's published example and mdxfind will not read it back in EITHER case, so the mdxfind mapping stays at tier `asserted`. relations.note: Measured 2026-09-05. At depth one the two are numerically identical -- SHA512RAWPASSSALT (e1013) and SHA512PASSSALT (e386) both compute sha512(pass . salt) -- and they diverge only from depth two, where e1013 feeds the RAW digest back and e386 feeds the hex. So they agree on exactly the depth-one inputs and nowhere else. A corpus-wide mdxfind sweep duly reports e1013 on this row's vector; that is the mask, not a mapping, and the tie breaks to the lower eN.

entries.name: SHA512RAWPASSSALT
entries.notes: Created 2026-09-05. Appendix A states the construction as sha512_bin(pass . salt) and glosses it "BlackBerry ES10 at -i 100". No denotation: is recorded because that is expressible and a denotation would foreclose it; run tools/derive-expressions.pl. Note what this row is NOT: at depth one it is numerically identical to SHA512PASSSALT (e386), which sha512-pass-salt and filezilla-server-ge-0-9-55 already carry, and the two differ only in ITERATION ROLE -- this one feeds the raw digest back. A corpus sweep will therefore report e1013 on those rows; that is the mask, not a mapping, and ties break to the lower eN.

relations.note: Measured 2026-09-05. At depth one the two are numerically identical -- SHA512RAWPASSSALT (e1013) and SHA512PASSSALT (e386) both compute sha512(pass . salt) -- and they diverge only from depth two, where e1013 feeds the RAW digest back and e386 feeds the hex. So they agree on exactly the depth-one inputs and nowhere else. A corpus-wide mdxfind sweep duly reports e1013 on this row's vector; that is the mask, not a mapping, and the tie breaks to the lower eN.

entries.expr_note: transcribed from the hx specification's Appendix A entry for mdxfind type WINPHONE (e928), which states sha256(utf16le(pass) . fromhex(salt)) (salt = 256-hex / 128 bytes). Transcription, not reproduction, so this is upstream and not vector; run derive-expressions.pl to try to promote it. Checked by hand on 2026-08-31 anyway: Digest::SHA -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes exactly this construction over the entry's own vector and reproduces its digest. That is corroboration, not tier 'vector', which requires john's own compiler; john has no fromhex() in its dynamic expression language, so derive-expressions.pl cannot promote this.; TRIAGE 2026-09-04 [corroborated]: no john format, so john ships no control vectors; but RosettaExpr -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes this expression over the entry's own vector(s) and reproduces 1 of 1. That is corroboration, not tier vector, which needs john's own compiler. The sentence "Not checkable locally: ... RosettaExpr cannot compile" was withdrawn on 2026-09-04: RosettaExpr was widened by sha224, sha384 and the utf16 family and compiles this expression, so the claim was false. The tier is untouched -- what changed is this repository's reach, not the evidence.

Transcription, not reproduction, so this is upstream and not vector; run derive-expressions.pl to try to promote it.; TRIAGE 2026-09-04 [no-john-format]: no john format on this entry, so john ships no control vectors, and the entry carries no vector of its own to check the expression against. RosettaExpr cannot compile" was withdrawn on 2026-09-04: RosettaExpr was widened by sha224, sha384 and the utf16 family and compiles this expression, so the claim was false.
